evidence: Cic. Or. 154: dein … prō deinde … dīcimus
terms.comment: The next step in a series: prīmum … deinde … tum. Dein is the short form, which Cicero notes is often said; in classical verse the ei of both makes one syllable (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Verg. G. 4.187: tum tēcta petunt, tum corpora cūrant
terms.comment: Both “at that time” and “next”; in a series it often follows prīmum or deinde.
Of a later time rather than the next step.

terms.gloss: after that, thereupon; from then on
the next thing is to …, the next point is
evidence: Cic. N.D. 2.73: proximum est, ut doceam deōrum prōvidentiā mundum administrārī (Lewis & Short s.v. propior)
Cic. Fl. 27: proximum est ergō, ut, opus fuerit classe necne, quaerāmus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Moving to the next step of an argument or a task. Traupman 102 gives it for “most likely”, which it does not mean (see probably).

terms.register: vōx cōmica et poētica: Enn., Plaut., Ter., Catull.
evidence: Plaut. Curc. 4.2.43: numquam postillā vīdī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Traupman writes postillāc, a form Lewis & Short does not give; the ante-classical and poetic word is postillā (or post illa). Prose says posteā.

phrases.latin: dā mī bāsia mīlle, deinde centum, dein mīlle altera, dein secunda centum
phrases.english: give me a thousand kisses, then a hundred, then another thousand, then a second hundred

phrases.latin: Homō est prīmum īnfāns, deinde puer, tum adulēscēns, inde juvenis, posteā vir, dehinc senex, tandem silicernium.
phrases.english: A person is first a baby, then a boy, then a youth, then a young man, then a man, then an old man, and at last a doddering ancient.
next comes …, then …, then …, after that …
